title: europe is underpricing its sweltering future 2026 08 18
author: Jon Sindreu
text:
LONDON, Aug 18 (Reuters Breakingviews) - Whether or not Europeans yield to the culture war and become less concerned about curbing climate change, this scorching-hot summer has underscored that they should spend way more money adapting to it. A ​temperature rise of 0.6 degrees Celsius per decade makes Europe the fastest warming
, opens new tab
 continent on Earth, yet only
, opens new tab
 23% of its households have ‌air conditioning (AC), compared with 90% in the United States. Closing this preparedness gap may cost much more than policymakers have budgeted.
Heatwaves have killed more than 25,000 people across Europe this year, Bloomberg estimates
, opens new tab
. Triodos Bank forecasts
, opens new tab
 they will cost the European Union's economy €180 billion, or 1% of GDP this year, in large part because worker productivity drops once temperatures rise above 25 ​C. Businesses can't fully protect against this: a new Moody's report argues that last summer's extreme weather generated only about €500 million of insured payouts ​despite costing Europeans €43 billion.
Meanwhile, EU lawmakers are walking
, opens new tab
 back some Net Zero commitments. This isn't fully irrational: Europe, which accounts ⁠for about 6% of global greenhouse gas emissions, can influence rising global temperatures only so much. Yet the European Commission's (EC) Clean Energy Investment Strategy still envisages
, opens new tab
 ​required public and private investments of nearly €700 billion a year in the 2030s.
That figure dwarfs what Europe plans to spend adapting to the climate change it can't ​prevent. Adaptation comes to €69 billion a year through 2050, a fraction of the mitigation spend. That’s the central forecast of a study
, opens new tab
 prepared for the EC by engineering consultancy Ricardo and the Euro-Mediterranean Centre on Climate Change, which is largely based on the priorities included in the adaptation strategies laid out by the EU's 27 member states themselves, with estimated ​costs scaled to reflect population, geography and climate-risk exposures. Infrastructure accounts for the largest share, at €29 billion annually, much of it for retrofitting buildings. London ​just provided an illustrative case from outside of the EU in saying
, opens new tab
 its Thames Barrier will need to be replaced sooner than expected.
Nevertheless, these estimates don't include specific measures to ‌install air ⁠conditioning in homes. Europeans have long resisted it, since temperatures often didn't justify the cost. But that is changing. Deadly heatwaves in the early 2000s drove Italians to embrace AC and the rest of Europe is likely to follow. Meanwhile, as India's experience suggests
, opens new tab
, people will use inefficient cooling units if they need to. It's far better to encourage usage of air-to-air pumps, which can also replace gas boilers in the winter.
Reaching U.S. AC adoption levels, however, would require refitting ​about 150 million homes, at €2,000 or ​more per installation. Add back-of-the-envelope estimates ⁠for maintenance, electricity, and power grid expenses, and the yearly adaptation bill could easily climb by an extra €30 billion. And that’s before accounting for cascading climate events or supply chain impacts.
In Europe, both climate change deniers and activists have ​long dismissed adaptation as too painful a compromise. Neither can avoid reckoning with its true costs anymore.
